title: Equity & Access: McKinney-Vento (Rights of Homeless Students)
author: Teach Beyond Borders
summary: This explainer for teachers sets out the McKinney-Vento Act and what it guarantees homeless children in US schools. It stresses that homelessness under the law covers anyone lacking a fixed, regular and adequate nighttime residence, so doubled-up families, motel residents and others count, and most homeless students look like every other child. It lists eight protections, including immediate enrollment without records, the right to stay in the school of origin with transport, a district liaison, free meals and full access to programmes. For teachers it describes signs such as sudden lateness, repeated new addresses and homework that never returns, advising teachers to notice and pass concerns to the liaison rather than investigate. It recommends asking about living situations in plain language, reviewing homework and late policies that assume a quiet home, and protecting privacy. It closes with the funding picture, noting that rights are law but money is a yearly fight.
points: A student who loses housing keeps the right to school, including immediate enrollment, staying at the school of origin and transport.
Most homeless students are doubled up and are invisible in the building, so teachers should know the signs and not rely on being told.
A teacher's job is to notice and pass information to the district liaison, not to investigate, and to keep housing status private.
Ask families about their living situation in plain terms rather than using the word homelessness.
Homework and lateness policies that assume a quiet table, Wi-Fi and a printer can penalise housing rather than measure learning.
quotes: If a child loses their housing, they don’t lose their right to school. The law makes schools clear away the paperwork, distance, and red tape that would otherwise push that child out.
Doubled up is by far the most common. Which means most homeless students in your building don’t match the picture in your head. They look like every other kid.

A school must enroll the student right away, even without the records it normally requires: proof of address, immunization records, birth certificate, transcripts, guardianship papers. The school chases the paperwork afterward. The kid sits in a classroom now.
You usually won’t be told. Housing status is confidential, and families often hide it out of fear or shame.
None of that proves anything. Your job isn’t to investigate. It’s to notice and pass it along to the liaison.

An assignment that assumes a quiet table, Wi-Fi, and a printer quietly penalizes the kids who don’t have them. A late penalty for a student who did homework in a motel room with four siblings measures housing, not learning.
A parent may say no to “Are you homeless?” and yes to “Are you staying with someone else right now?
The rights in McKinney-Vento are law. The money to carry them out is a separate fight every year.
